routes.description: Establish historical reliability through a cumulative standard that permits ordinary reporting variation while requiring substantial accuracy across the Gospels' claims.
routes.successCriteria: Show that verified or conceded claims at several levels outweigh alleged errors and that prominent discrepancies can arise from historically permissible conventions or reconcilable sequences.

motionBridge.description: The Gospels remain historically reliable if their supported historical content is not counterbalanced by established errors.

centralBridges.description: Identify substantial accurate content among major, intermediate, and lesser Gospel claims.
Show that the principal birth and resurrection differences do not negate the shared central claims or require incompatible histories.
Establish a historically supportable continuity between Synoptic material and claims about Jesus' elevated or divine identity.
Provide a plausible account of how traditions and sources preserved the essential events and teachings reported by the evangelists.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish selection, paraphrase, topical ordering, and approximation from factual contradiction.
Connect disputed material to eyewitnesses, remembered traditions, or sources close to eyewitness testimony.

routes.description: Establish historical unreliability in important respects by locating conflicts or inventions in major narratives and sayings rather than merely peripheral details.
routes.successCriteria: Show that major birth, resurrection, and self-presentation material cannot all be historically accurate and that authorial reshaping or unstable transmission explains the divergences.

motionBridge.description: The Gospels are historically unreliable in important respects if major reported events or sayings contain unresolved conflicts or nonhistorical material.

centralBridges.description: Demonstrate materially incompatible historical sequences within the canonical birth narratives.
Demonstrate materially incompatible locations, instructions, or actions within the resurrection narratives.
Show that John's divine self-presentation lacks adequate continuity with earlier Synoptic portrayals of Jesus.
Connect Gospel divergences to evangelists altering inherited material for distinct theological messages and audiences.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Assess whether narrow or nonindependent attestation weakens disputed claims.
Account for how decades of oral transmission and later composition could change reported events or sayings.

sectionSelections.title: Standard and cumulative case for reliability
sectionSelections.rationale: The governing definition of historical reliability determines whether conceded accuracy across much of Jesus' life can be outweighed by conflicts involving several major narratives or sayings.

proSelections.proposition: Historical reliability is distinct from inerrancy and may be established through many verified major, intermediate, and lesser claims unless contrary errors outweigh them.
The Gospels preserve many accurate lesser details, and the alleged errors presented do not counterbalance the cumulative accuracy of their major, intermediate, and lesser claims.

conSelections.proposition: Although the Gospels preserve a reliable basic outline of Jesus' life, numerous inconsistencies and nonhistorical accounts make them historically unreliable in important respects.
Agreement on many general facts does not establish Gospel reliability because conflicts concerning the virgin birth, resurrection, and Jesus' self-presentation concern major claims.

sectionSelections.title: Historical compatibility of the birth narratives
sectionSelections.rationale: Matthew and Luke are the canonical sources that narrate Jesus' birth, so the compatibility and provenance of their family movements bear directly on a principal alleged instance of unreliability.

proSelections.proposition: The birth accounts can be reconciled if Joseph had connections or property in Bethlehem while living and working in Nazareth before the family's later return there.
Luke's infancy narratives plausibly preserve memories ultimately originating with Mary, although Luke need not have interviewed her personally or used her for the whole Gospel.

conSelections.proposition: Matthew's and Luke's birth narratives give incompatible accounts of the family's original home, travel, census, flight to Egypt, and eventual settlement in Nazareth.
A lower-class manual laborer in first-century Palestine would be unlikely to maintain residences in both Bethlehem and Nazareth, making that reconciliation historically implausible.

sectionSelections.title: Compatibility of the resurrection accounts
sectionSelections.rationale: The resurrection is a central Gospel claim, making the chronology and locations of the women's report, appearances, and disciples' movements material to the reliability question.

proSelections.proposition: All four Gospels affirm the resurrection, so disagreements about surrounding narrative details do not by themselves negate that shared major claim.
The Jerusalem and Galilee traditions are compatible if appearances occurred first in Jerusalem, later in Galilee, and subsequently again in Jerusalem.

conSelections.proposition: The resurrection narratives cannot all be reconciled regarding whether the women reported the empty tomb and whether the disciples remained in Jerusalem or traveled to Galilee.
The resurrection narratives disagree over whether the disciples remained in Jerusalem or went to Galilee and over where Jesus appeared.

sectionSelections.title: Jesus' self-presentation and divine identity
sectionSelections.rationale: Whether John's divine self-identifications preserve Jesus' historical teaching depends partly on whether earlier Synoptic traditions contain comparable claims, directly or indirectly.

proSelections.proposition: The Synoptic Gospels indirectly portray Jesus as divine, especially when Mark's trial scene associates him with Daniel's enthroned Son of Man and a blasphemy charge.

conSelections.proposition: John's extensive divine self-identification by Jesus is historically doubtful because multiple earlier Synoptic sources do not portray him making comparable claims.
Mark's trial statement does not explicitly identify Jesus himself as the coming Son of Man, so it cannot securely establish that Jesus claimed divinity there.

sectionSelections.title: Ancient composition and transmission
sectionSelections.rationale: The reliability inference depends on whether variation reflects permissible ancient reporting and stable preservation or instead historical invention, changing oral tradition, and message-driven alteration.

proSelections.proposition: Ancient Gospel accounts ordinarily convey an accurate gist with approximate details, so evaluating them as if they promised modern precision can generate false contradictions.
The Gospel tradition was preserved by motivated believers who retained its gist, and the canonical accounts stand close to eyewitness sources rather than a long telephone chain.

conSelections.proposition: Ancient biography is frequently historically unreliable, and lengthy speeches attributed to Jesus decades later by non-eyewitnesses cannot be assumed to reproduce what he said.
The evangelists primarily proclaimed theological messages to Christian audiences and changed inherited material rather than pursuing historical accuracy in the modern sense.
